title: LDraw Geometry Kernel & Instanced LOD Pipeline

cells.source:
# LDraw Geometry Kernel & Instanced LOD Pipeline

Draw a brick city in 3D and the studs cost far more than the bricks. A brick's box is 12 triangles, but each round stud is 48, so the eight studs on a 2 × 4 brick are 384 triangles: 97% of the brick. 3D brick viewers built on the LDraw parts library tame big scenes with three tricks before anything reaches the graphics card:

1. **Skip hidden studs.** A stud with a brick on top of it can't be seen, so don't draw it.
2. **Simplify distant studs**, known as *level of detail* (LOD): 16-sided studs close to the viewer, 6-sided ones further off, and none at all in the distance, where a stud would be a pixel or two.
3. **Draw alike things together.** three.js's `InstancedMesh` draws every brick body in one go, and every stud of each kind in another, instead of one call per object.

C builds a city block of 200 bricks and counts the triangles each trick saves. A chart compares the stages, three.js draws the city, and a last chart shows how the LOD distance setting trades detail for triangles.

How the cells run:

- **C runs in your browser.** The cell is compiled to WebAssembly by xcc, on the page, and runs at once, on the website too.
- **C reads the controls with `nb_get_int` and `nb_get_number`.** After changing the culling or the distance bias, press **▶** on the C cell; the colour and wireframe settings work straight away.
- **Distances are measured from a fixed viewpoint** at the front-right street corner, not from the 3D view's camera, so the detail levels stay put as you orbit.

> ✨ The code cells were written by an AI model from prompts, and each prompt is saved in its cell: press **✨** in a cell's header to see it.

Press **Run all**.

## 2. Build the city and count the triangles in C

> In C, build a small brick city block on a grid 20 × 20 studs and 14 layers high: a paved base with a road and a crossing, a red café with windows and a door, a blue townhouse with a clock tower and a red spire, two street lights and a fountain. Read lod_cull_hidden and lod_dist_scale from nb with <nb.h>. For every stud, note whether a brick covers it, and give each brick a detail level from its distance to a viewpoint at the front-right street corner, (18, 6, 20), divided by the bias: LOD 0 under 12.5, LOD 1 under 20, LOD 2 beyond. Count triangles at 12 per brick body and 48, 18 or 0 per visible stud, and print the bill at four stages: everything at full detail, hidden studs skipped, detail levels applied, and bodies alone. Share nb.lod_scene with the counts and every brick's position, colour, level and visible studs as a bitmask.

- **`occ`** is the city as a 3D grid: which colour of brick fills each stud and layer, or 0. A stud is hidden when the cell right above it is filled.
- **`place_brick`** refuses a brick that would overlap another, so the city can be described in loops without checking every brick by hand.
- **`exposed_mask`** keeps one bit per stud on top of a brick: 1 if it's drawn. The 3D view uses it to know which studs to draw.

## 5. How much detail?

> Using nb.lod_scene's bricks and their visible studs, work out the triangle bill for every LOD distance bias from 0.4 to 2 in steps of 0.1, the way the C cell does (distance from (18, 6, 20); LOD 0 under 12.5 × bias, LOD 1 under 20 × bias). Print the totals at the smallest, current and largest bias, and whether the current one matches the C cell. Return a Vega-Lite stacked area chart of the triangles from brick bodies, close studs and middle studs against the bias, with a line at the current bias.

The distance bias is a dial between looks and speed. A bias of 2 keeps detail twice as far away; 0.4 throws most of it out. This cell tries every setting without running the C cell again.

## What the run shows

- **Studs are nearly the whole bill.** The block has 200 bricks with 1,250 places for a stud. At full detail that's 62,400 triangles, and the brick bodies are only 2,400 of them.
- **Hidden studs are most of the studs.** 790 of the 1,250 (63%) have a brick on top. Skipping them brings the bill down to 24,480, 61% less, and the picture doesn't change at all.
- **Detail levels halve it again.** Of the 460 studs left, 117 are close (16 sides), 261 further off (6 sides) and 82 far enough to drop, for 12,714 triangles: 79.6% below where it started.
- **The tricks work together.** Without skipping hidden studs, detail levels alone get to 26,562, more than twice as many.
- **The bias is a dial from 3,120 to 24,330 triangles.** At 0.4 almost only the bodies are left; at 2 nearly every visible stud is drawn at full detail.

## Try this

Each of these is a prompt. Press **✨** in a cell's header to change its prompt and generate it again, or **⚡ AI Generate New Cell** at the bottom to add a new one.

- **See the levels.** Switch **3D Shader Mode** to the heat map, then **Mesh Wireframe** to wireframe, and compare the studs close up with those further away.
- **Draw every stud.** Set **Hidden-Stud Occlusion** to disabled and press **▶** on the C cell, then on the charts. How much does skipping hidden studs really save?
- **A bigger city.** Press ✨ on the C cell and add: *"Add a second street of three more buildings behind the first."* Which trick saves the most as the city grows?
- **Understand the code.** Press the speech bubble (**Explain this cell**) on the C cell and ask how `exposed_mask` records which studs to draw.
